name: Professor Aldric Vane
equipment: Arcane focus (crystal sphere with swirling silver interior)
A letter from a dead colleague
A set of planar cartography tools
features: Arcane Recovery (once per day after a short rest, recover expended spell slots with a combined level equal to or less than half your wizard level rounded up — up to 4 levels of spell slots; no slot recovered can be 6th level or higher)
Conjuration Savant (the gold and time required to copy conjuration spells into your spellbook is halved)

Minor Conjuration (as an action, conjure an inanimate object in your hand or on the ground in an unoccupied space within 10 feet; the object can be no larger than 3 feet on a side and weigh no more than 10 pounds; it must be in the form of a nonmagical object you have seen; the object is visibly magical, radiating dim light out to 5 feet; it disappears after 1 hour, when you use this feature again, or when it takes or deals any damage)

Benign Transposition (as an action, teleport up to 30 feet to an unoccupied space you can see, OR swap places with a willing Small or Medium creature within 30 feet; once used, you cannot use this feature again until you finish a long rest or cast a conjuration spell of 1st level or higher)

Researcher (Sage feature: when you attempt to learn or recall a piece of lore, if you do not know that information, you often know where and from whom you can obtain it; usually from a library, scriptorium, university, or a sage or other learned person or creature)
Ability Score Improvements (levels 4 and 8: +2 Intelligence at each, raising INT from 16 to 20)

personality.traits: Aldric speaks with the rapid, digressive cadence of a man who has spent thirty years lecturing to students who cannot keep up. He begins sentences on one topic and arrives at a completely different one, connected by a chain of associations that makes perfect sense to him and bewilders everyone else. He has a habit of narrating his own thought process aloud — 'Now, if we consider the planar membrane as a function of ambient thaumic pressure, which of course implies that the local leyline density must be...' — trailing off when he reaches a conclusion, forgetting that no one else followed the journey. He is perpetually patting his pockets for things he has misplaced, adjusting spectacles he no longer wears (he cast a permanent Darkvision ritual on himself years ago and discarded them, but the habit remains), and scribbling notes in the margins of whatever he happens to be holding, including other people's belongings. Despite his scattered exterior, his mind is extraordinarily organized — he simply operates on a level of complexity that makes ordinary conversation feel reductive.
personality.ideals: Knowledge without application is merely trivia, and application without ethics is merely destruction. Aldric believes that the purpose of scholarship is to understand the world well enough to protect it — that every theorem, every discovery, every late night spent cross-referencing planar topology maps is justified only if it ultimately serves the living. He has watched too many of his colleagues retreat into pure theory, publishing papers that no one reads about phenomena that no one cares about, while the real multiverse burned around them. The Convergence is the vindication of everything he has argued for decades: that planar studies is not an abstract discipline but a survival science, and that someone who understands the math needs to be standing at the fracture point when the equations go wrong. He does not believe he is the smartest person in any room, but he believes he is often the only person in the room willing to translate intelligence into action.
personality.bonds: Aldric's colleague and closest friend, Professor Elara Nighthollow, was the first to detect the mathematical signature of the Convergence — an anomalous recursion in the equations governing planar boundary tension. She sent Aldric her findings in a letter that arrived three days after her death. She had gone to investigate a planar fracture near the Ashfell Mountains and never returned. The letter, stained with coffee and covered in her characteristic cramped handwriting, sits in Aldric's breast pocket. He reads it every morning. Finding out what happened to Elara — whether she is dead, trapped between planes, or something stranger — is the personal thread that pulls him through every danger. He also carries a deep loyalty to the University of Argentmere, which gave a poor fisherman's son a scholarship and a purpose, and he hopes to return someday with enough knowledge to ensure the Convergence never threatens the mortal world again.
personality.flaws: Aldric is a chronic underestimator of physical danger. He has spent so long in the safe, controlled environment of a university that he sometimes forgets the Astral Sea is not a classroom — that the creatures he has studied in textbooks are real, and they do not care about his tenure or his publication record. He takes unnecessary risks to gather data, lingers too long examining phenomena that are actively trying to kill him, and occasionally prioritizes intellectual curiosity over tactical common sense. He is also deeply insecure about his physical limitations — he is not young, not strong, and not particularly brave, and he compensates by being aggressively useful in every other way, sometimes to the point of exhausting himself. He has a quiet terror of being seen as a burden by his more physically capable companions, which leads him to volunteer for tasks he should probably leave to others and to downplay injuries and fatigue until they become dangerous.

appearance: Professor Aldric Vane is a man in his early fifties who looks every year of it and has long since stopped caring. He stands five feet eight inches tall, with a thin, wiry frame that suggests he regularly forgets to eat — which he does, often going an entire day on nothing but tea and absent-minded handfuls of trail mix before someone reminds him that mortals require sustenance. His hair is a disheveled mane of steel grey, once dark brown, swept back from a high forehead and perpetually looking as though he has just been standing in a strong wind or has recently exploded something. His face is narrow and angular, with sharp cheekbones, a long nose, deep-set eyes of a vivid, almost unsettling blue — the kind of blue that makes people wonder if there is a spell involved (there is not) — and a neatly trimmed goatee that is the one part of his appearance he maintains with any consistency. His hands are his most notable feature after his eyes: long-fingered, ink-stained, and never still, always gesturing, sketching diagrams in the air, or manipulating the crystal sphere he uses as an arcane focus — a beautiful object the size of a large orange, filled with slowly swirling silver mist that responds to his emotional state, churning faster when he is excited and going perfectly still when he is afraid. He dresses in the rumpled academic robes he wore at the university, modified for travel with practical additions: reinforced hems, deeper pockets (so many pockets), a belt hung with pouches of spell components, and sturdy boots that look painfully new, as though he purchased them specifically for this journey and has not yet broken them in. His spellbook hangs from a chain at his hip like a soldier's sword — a thick, battered leather volume covered in hand-drawn planar diagrams, its pages stuffed with loose notes, pressed flowers from other planes, and the occasional sandwich wrapper. A pair of brass-rimmed spectacles sits perpetually on top of his head, serving no optical purpose whatsoever but providing a convenient place to rest his fingers when he is thinking. The silver compass shard — his Threadwalker focus — is embedded in the cover of his spellbook, glinting faintly with its own inner light.
backstory:
Aldric Vane grew up in a fishing village on the Cormorant Coast, the son of a net-mender and a woman who cleaned fish for the market. His childhood was salt air, rough hands, and the bone-deep certainty that his life would consist of boats, nets, and the grey expanse of the sea until he was too old to haul rope. He was not unhappy with this prospect — his parents were kind, the work was honest, and the sea had its own austere beauty. What changed everything was a book.

A merchant ship ran aground on the rocks near the village during a storm, and young Aldric, twelve years old, was among the villagers who helped salvage what they could. In the wreckage, he found a water-damaged copy of 'Fundamentals of Planar Theory' by Archmage Perault. Most of the pages were illegible, but enough survived to ignite something in the boy's mind that had never been lit before. The idea that reality was not a single, solid thing but a layered construction of overlapping planes — that the ground beneath his feet was just one page in an infinite book — struck him with the force of religious revelation.

He taught himself to read the surviving pages. He pestered the village herbalist, the only educated person for miles, until she taught him basic magical theory. At sixteen, he walked forty miles to the nearest city and presented himself at the academy, where a bemused admissions clerk gave him an entrance examination more out of curiosity than expectation. Aldric scored the highest marks the academy had seen in a decade. A scholarship was arranged. His mother cried. His father shook his hand and told him to come home sometimes.

Aldric spent the next three decades in academia, rising from student to professor to department chair of Planar Studies at the University of Argentmere. He was not the most powerful wizard on the faculty — his talent lay not in raw magical force but in understanding, in the ability to see patterns in planar topology that others missed, to build mathematical models that predicted how the boundaries between worlds would behave under stress. He published extensively, corresponded with scholars across the continent, and developed a reputation as the foremost theoretical authority on planar boundary mechanics — a niche so specialized that his colleagues joked that his field had an audience of exactly three people, two of whom were his graduate students.

He chose the School of Conjuration because conjuration is, at its core, the magic of boundaries — of reaching across the membrane between here and there and pulling something through. Every conjuration spell is a controlled planar breach, and Aldric studied them the way a structural engineer studies controlled demolitions: to understand what holds things together by understanding exactly how they come apart.

The Convergence announced itself in his equations before it manifested in reality. His colleague Elara Nighthollow — brilliant, reckless, the only person who could follow his mathematical reasoning without a three-hour tutorial — noticed it first: a recursive anomaly in the boundary tension equations, a pattern that should have been impossible, suggesting that something was systematically weakening the planar membranes from the spaces between them. She wrote to Aldric immediately and then, because she was Elara and patience was not among her virtues, went to investigate a planar fracture near the Ashfell Mountains without waiting for his response.

Her letter arrived three days after word of her death. Or rather, three days after word of her disappearance — her expedition found the fracture, and then the fracture found them. The site was empty when the rescue party arrived. No bodies, no equipment, no tracks. Just a patch of ground where the grass grew in spirals and the air tasted like silver.

Aldric read Elara's letter seventeen times. On the eighteenth reading, he packed a bag, resigned his position, and walked out of the university. His colleagues were bewildered. His students were abandoned mid-semester. The department chair appointment he had held for eleven years was left vacant with a one-paragraph letter of resignation that said, simply: 'The math requires my presence elsewhere. I apologize for the inconvenience.'

The journey to the Astral Sea nearly killed him four times. Aldric was not an adventurer. He was a middle-aged academic with bad knees and a theoretical understanding of danger that bore no resemblance to the reality of being chased through a collapsing planar rift by something with too many teeth. But his knowledge of planar topology allowed him to navigate the fractures that the Convergence was tearing in reality, stepping through weakened boundaries that would have shredded a less knowledgeable traveler, until he stumbled — literally, face-first — through the threshold of the Citadel and into the presence of the Astral Wardens.

The githzerai were skeptical of the disheveled human who claimed to understand their ancient enemy through mathematics. Then Aldric spent three hours at a chalkboard demonstrating that the Convergence followed a predictable pattern — that the planar fractures were not random but were converging on specific nodes, and that he could predict where the next one would appear. The Wardens stopped being skeptical. Master Zerith-Ka named him a Threadwalker, and Aldric — who had never been brave, never been strong, never been anything except relentlessly, obsessively curious — accepted the charge with the quiet determination of a man who understands that the equations do not care whether he is afraid.
